title: Two Economic Thermometers-One Confused Wall Street
summary: Consumer confidence measures improvement, but household budgets reflect reality. Here's why that distinction matters for stocks and the Fed.
body_markdown:
*Consumer confidence measures improvement, but household budgets reflect reality. Here's why that distinction matters for stocks and the Fed.*


***KEY TAKEAWAYS***


-


Consumer Confidence delivered a massive upside surprise. The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index jumped 11.4 points to 103.3 in November, exceeding every economist's forecast in Bloomberg's survey.


-


Consumer sentiment remains historically depressed. The University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index improved to 51.5 in November but remains in the bottom 1% of its historical readings.


-


Stock market performance is influencing household finances. While 51.6% of Conference Board respondents expect stock prices to rise over the next year, Michigan reported deteriorating personal finances among consumers with the largest stock holdings.


-


Holiday spending is expected to rise despite fewer shoppers. The National Retail Federation forecasts $1.013 trillion in holiday sales, representing 4.2% annual growth, while Thanksgiving weekend shopper numbers are expected to decline to 182.7 million.


-


Today's inflation report will provide another measure of consumer health. Economists expect October headline PCE inflation to accelerate to 3.8% and core PCE inflation to rise to 3.2%, with the report also providing inflation-adjusted personal spending data.


***MY HOT TAKES***


-


A consumer can be confident without being financially comfortable. Improving employment prospects are encouraging, but having a paycheck and being able to afford your lifestyle are two entirely different economic conditions.


-


Wall Street is confusing direction with level. Falling gasoline prices and moderating inflation expectations represent genuine improvements, but neither erases the cumulative financial burden that households have absorbed.


-


The wealth effect is becoming an increasingly important consumer risk. When higher-income households increasingly anchor their financial well-being to their brokerage statements, stock market weakness can quickly become a discretionary spending problem.


-


A bargain-hunting consumer is not necessarily bullish for retail stocks. Strong store traffic and rising nominal revenues may conceal deteriorating pricing power, aggressive discounting, and pressure on gross margins.


-


Black Friday's sales headlines deserve a healthy dose of skepticism. Investors should focus on merchandise volumes, inflation-adjusted spending, and sustainable profitability rather than celebrating record dollar sales in an inflationary economy.


-


You can quote me: *“Yesterday’s confidence number took its reading up top, where the jobs are plentiful and the portfolios were, until recently, nice and toasty. The registers are on the middle rack.”*


***My oven lies.*** I have known this for years. Set it to 350 and the display says 350–proudly, I might add. But hanging off the middle rack is a six dollar thermometer, and that little thing says… *325* ! Same oven. Same moment. Two numbers. On an ordinary Wednesday, who cares? But tomorrow is Thanksgiving, and as many of you know, the bird is MY thing. Twenty-five degrees is the difference between a hero and a guy ordering pizza for twenty. 🤣 So which one do I believe? The one built into the appliance to make me feel good about the appliance, or the one that just hangs there and reports? Yesterday we learned that Consumer Confidence jumped to its highest level in almost two years. A few days earlier, another well-known gauge of the VERY same consumer came in near the bottom of its entire history. Same consumer. Same month. Two numbers. 🤔


Let me start with the display, because it is the number everybody saw. The Conference Board–a business research group that has been taking the American consumer’s temperature for at least my whole career on Wall Street (and well before)–said yesterday that its Consumer Confidence Index jumped 11.4 points in November to 103.3. Economists were looking for something near 92. It beat EVERY forecast in Bloomberg’s survey–Wells Fargo analysts were the most bullish expecting 94.7, so, yeah it was a solid beat. It was also its best reading since January of 2025. Now look at where it came from. In September–two months ago mind you–this very same index sat at its lowest level since April of 2014. So in about sixty days we went from the gloomiest consumer in more than a decade to the cheeriest in almost two years. Ovens do not heat up that fast. 🧐


What changed? Jobs, mostly. Some 30.8% of those surveyed said jobs are plentiful, up from 26.2% in October, and the share calling jobs hard to get fell to 18.4% from 21.4%. The part of the index that looks six months ahead climbed to 83.6–the first time all year it has been above 80, the line the Conference Board has said in the past signals a recession ahead. The Board’s own economist offered a simple explanation: less uncertainty now that the midterm elections are over. That makes sense to me. The ads stop, the phone stops ringing, and everybody exhales–no matter who they voted for.


Now the six dollar thermometer. Last Friday the University of Michigan published its final November reading on the same consumer. It improved too–to 51.5 from 48.0. A word of caution. These two surveys are built on different scales, so you cannot set 103 next to 51 and call it a day. What you CAN do is compare each one to its own history. The Conference Board’s number is at a nearly two-year high. Michigan’s sits in the bottom 1% of every reading that survey has ever produced. One gauge says the oven is hot. The other says you may want to keep your coat on.


How can both be right? Because they are not asking the same question. The Conference Board leans on jobs and business conditions. Michigan leans on personal finances and prices. One is asking, more or less, can you find work? The other is asking, can you afford your life? In November of 2026, an awful lot of Americans would answer yes to the first and…well, something less polite to the second. 😊


Now, there is a detail in each report that I would circle if I were you. The Conference Board said the improvement was biggest among higher-income households. It also found 51.6% of consumers expecting stock prices to RISE over the next year–the long-run average, according to my friend and legendary economist Ed Yardeni, is closer to 36%. Michigan, meanwhile, reported that the consumers with the largest stock holdings said their personal finances got WORSE in November, and it pointed to the stock market. Ya think??? 🤣🤣 Confident and feeling poorer, in the same month! Those are the households retailers count on for the expensive stuff, and their mood is now tied to a brokerage statement. The S&P 500 has fallen in eight of the last nine sessions. We call this the wealth effect (people spend more freely when their portfolios are up, and less freely when they are not). It works in both directions.


So what are these gauges really measuring? Take gasoline. The national average dropped 56 cents a gallon in the first 24 days of November–the biggest such drop on record. That feels WONDERFUL. It is also true that at $3.62 on Tuesday you are paying about sixty cents more than you did last Thanksgiving, and this holiday is in the running to be the most expensive ever at the pump. Both statements are facts. One is the DIRECTION. The other is the LEVEL.


The same thing shows up inside the confidence report itself. Consumers now expect inflation of 5.7% over the next year. That is down for a second straight month. Improvement! It is also 5.7%, in a country whose central bank is aiming for 2–in case you forgot. And when the Conference Board let people write in their own comments, they were still grumbling about high prices. Confidence, it turns out, is a measure of direction. It tells you whether things feel better than they did last month. Your checking account does not care about last month. It pays the level.


So let’s go where the level gets paid–the register. Retail sales rose 0.2% in October, and the Census Bureau’s own margin of error on that figure is plus or minus 0.4. In plain English, the government is not certain that sales rose at all. To be fair, the part of the report economists trust most (the so-called control group, which strips out cars, gasoline, building materials, and restaurants) rose a healthy 0.6%. Not a collapse. But neither…a boom.


For the holidays, the National Retail Federation is forecasting sales of $1.013 trillion in November and December, up 4.2% from last year. It also expects 182.7 million people to shop this weekend–DOWN from 186.9 million a year ago. More dollars. Fewer shoppers. And with prices running 3.6% above last year by the Fed’s favorite gauge, a good chunk of that 4.2% is just the price tag.


Yesterday’s earnings told me who is winning. Kohl’s reported its first increase in comparable sales after EIGHTEEN straight quarterly declines, and the stock jumped better than 19%. What did management talk about? Shoppers hunting for affordability. Dollar Tree gained 11%. Best Buy posted comparable-sales growth north of 6%–its best in five years–and then guided to 2% to 4% for the holiday quarter. Abercrombie & Fitch raised its forecast and soared about 20%, though some $120 million in tariff refunds helped the margins along. More found money, as I wrote in last week’s blog post. 😉


Here is why that matters to you as an investor. A confident consumer who is hunting for bargains is a very different animal from a confident consumer who is splurging. The first one shows up–the parking lot looks great–and then squeezes the retailer on price. So when the holiday results roll in, I will be skipping right past the sales line and reading three others. Did the growth come from more items in the bag, or just higher prices? What happened to gross margin (what a retailer keeps after paying for the merchandise) once the discounting started? And how much of the profit came from one-time items like those refunds? Sales tell you the store was busy. Margins tell you whether it was worth opening the doors.


The actual temperature arrives at 8:30 Wall Street Time, this morning–after this note is already in your hot little hands. That is when the government releases October's Personal Income and Spending report, and tucked inside it is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge (PCE). Economists expect the core rate, which leaves out food and energy, to tick UP to 3.2% from 3.1%, and the headline rate to climb to 3.8% from 3.6%. But the line I will be reading first is spending AFTER inflation. If Americans bought more stuff in October, the display deserves more credit than I have given it. If they simply paid more for the same stuff, the six-dollar thermometer wins another round.


I am not here to spoil anybody’s holiday. Confidence going up beats confidence going down–every time–and gas at $3.62 beats gas at $4.30, which is where it was in mid-October. Americans feel better than they did in September, and they have earned it.


But I learned something about my oven the hard way. The display is not lying, exactly. It takes its reading from a sensor up top, in the warmest corner of the box. The six-dollar thermometer hangs on the middle rack–where the bird is. Yesterday’s confidence number took its reading up top, where the jobs are plentiful and the portfolios were, until recently, nice and toasty. The registers are on the middle rack.


So tomorrow I will do what I do every year. I will set the dial, ignore it completely, and trust the cheap thermometer. Around four o’clock my family will render its verdict on the turkey, and no display on earth will save me. On Friday morning the American consumer renders hers. I will be watching the registers–right after the leftovers. And if the bird comes out dry? I am blaming the oven. 😉 Happy Thanksgiving. 🦃


***YESTERDAY’S MARKETS***


*Stocks finished mixed on Tuesday as the rebound in artificial-intelligence shares faded, with the S&P 500 down 0.50% and the Nasdaq Composite down 1.48%. A 423 point advance left the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 50,019. Nvidia shares fell 5.9% and technology lost more than 3%, while health care led the gainers and the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index rose to 103.3. Crude finished higher, with West Texas Intermediate up 2.35% at $82.05 a barrel, while the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.90%.*


***NEXT UP***


-


Personal Income (October) may have risen by 0.4% after climbing by 0.2% in the prior month.


-


Personal Spending (October) probably rose by 0.4% after increasing by 0.5% in September.


-


PCE Price Index (October) may have sped up to 3.8% from 3.6%.


-


Annualized Quarterly GDP (Q3) may be revised up to 3.5% from 3.4%.


-


Initial Jobless Claims (Nov 21) are expected to come in at 200k after gaining 2.3k claims in the prior month.


-


Markets are closed for Thanksgiving tomorrow but open for a truncated session on Friday. When we hit the ground running next week, the heavier versions of ourselves will encounter still more earning, JOLTS, ISM PMIs, Factory Orders, Nonfarm Payrolls, Unemployment Rate, and University of Michigan Sentiment. Don’t overcook the turkey–rely on what you know works–come and get it here.
